results.summary: This design simulates Conway's Game of Life on a 32x16 grid with periodic boundary conditions. It outputs the state to an ANSI serial terminal over UART and also provides VGA output via the bidirectional pins. The initial state is pseudo-randomly generated using an LFSR, and the simulation can be controlled via single-character commands over UART. Silicon testing confirmed that the terminal output works as expected.

This is a chess move generator implemented in SystemVerilog. It uses a 256-bit chessboard and a 64-bit square-enable mask to compute attacks and arbitrate the most promising move. The design is intended to be driven by an external RP2040 microprocessor, as the chip lacks the space to run the full game logic. It is tested using a provided test suite.

This project implements a 256-byte ROM that stores information about the Tiny Tapeout chip. The ROM is 8 bits wide and is accessed by setting the address pins and reading the data pins. The first 16 bytes are 7-segment encoded and contain the shuttle name and commit hash, which can be displayed on the on-board 7-segment display. No external hardware is required beyond the standard board.

This is a proof-of-concept experiment with GDS-level open-source countermeasure implementation. It exposes a set of customized hardened matrices that can be selected via the MAT_SEL input. The design is intended for fab testing and research purposes, allowing comparison of the observed input-to-output mapping with a reference model. No external hardware is required.

This design generates a PRBS31 signal using a Fibonacci LFSR and also analyzes it with a similar structure. It includes two 7-bit vectors that are converted to pseudo-random signals by comparison with the PRBS, which can be used as an alternative to a PWM DAC. A 131-bit PRBS generator is also included. The design requires an external ADALM2000 for testing.

This project implements a single NAND gate that is time-multiplexed using a giant shift register to emulate complex logic. The design achieves a time/space tradeoff by feeding inputs from and writing results to the shift register. It requires an external FPGA or similar to drive the inputs at high precision to feed instructions. Silicon testing showed it works as expected even at high frequencies.

This analog project generates two sinusoidal oscillators centered around 0.9V, targeting 20MHz and 21MHz. The oscillators are based on ring oscillators and should oscillate regardless of chip corner, though frequency varies. Silicon testing showed they run slower than intended (approx 13 and 14.2MHz) with waveforms between sinusoidal and triangular. No external hardware is required for operation.

This is an all-digital delay-locked loop (DLL) test design featuring tunable, hierarchical oscillation blocks. It demonstrates a clock generator and a 90-degree delay line using delay elements and control registers. The design is validated in TSMC-28 and is being tested on open tools and an open PDK. It requires an external oscilloscope for visualizing waveforms and uses bsg_tag for hardware testing.

This design is a fast magnitude comparator intended for digital neuron threshold detection. It compares two 8-bit inputs and outputs less-than, equal, and greater-than signals. The design is based on a bit-sliced expandable structure expressed in AND-INV form to leverage ABC9 logic optimization. Silicon testing confirmed correct operation, though documentation on output bit mapping was unclear.

This project implements a Manchester decoder and parser for 433MHz transmissions, such as those from a thermostat. It uses two state machines: one for decoding the Manchester signal and another for parsing the data frames. The decoded data is accessible via parallel output lines based on an address. External hardware required is a 433MHz receiver connected to the digital input pin.
